label: Feedback resilience
summary: Feedback resilience is the ability to receive critical feedback on your writing without taking it personally or reacting defensively. It rests on practising detachment from your texts, so that your content is treated as a product rather than an extension of your identity. In Maaike's framing, this resilience is something that develops gradually through writing as a craft and building consistent writing routines.
how_maaike_uses: Maaike grounds feedback resilience in a very practical, hard-won place: years of red pens and angry circles taught her that emotional over-attachment to texts is a risk, not an inevitability. She treats detachment as something you can actively practise in the moment, for instance by taking written notes during feedback conversations, which occupies enough mental capacity to crowd out emotional reactions. She also reframes feedback as a signal that your client actually read and cared about the work, and frames the writing relationship as a system with quality parameters you can discuss and agree on, rather than a judgement of you as a person. The more you write, she argues, the easier this gets, because writing becomes less of a high-stakes personal event and more of a repeatable craft.
open_questions: How do you build detachment early in your writing practice, before years of experience have made it more automatic?
The post gestures at a practical follow-up but cuts off. What concrete techniques or frameworks does Maaike use when actually negotiating feedback with a client?
